name: Unsaturated Polyester (UP): a Fiberglass Revolution
notation_note: The linear prepolymer is shown. Its point is the carbon-carbon double bond in every repeat: dissolved styrene adds across those bonds during cure and staples the chains into a network.
historical_events_referenced: Surrender of German forces at the Battle of Stalingrad (2 February 1943)
The Battle of the Atlantic and 'Black May' 1943

historical_images.alt: A long column of German prisoners of war, heavily bundled against the cold, walking past the bombed and shell-pocked ruins of a large grain elevator building in the snow.
historical_images.caption: German prisoners marched through Stalingrad after the February 1943 surrender — one of the two fronts on which the war's balance visibly shifted that year.
historical_images.author: Soviet military personnel (uncredited)

historical_images.alt: An aerial view of the ocean surface with a German U-boat under attack, a large plume of white water and spray thrown up beside its hull from a depth-charge or bomb strike.
historical_images.caption: A U-boat under attack from an RAF Coastal Command aircraft, 24 June 1943 — the kind of aircraft-borne radar sortie that closed the mid-Atlantic gap, and the kind of housing problem that unsaturated polyester and glass fiber were pressed into service to solve.
historical_images.author: Australian armed forces

historical_images.alt: Tall cylindrical steel storage silos and elevated walkways at an industrial batch house, with smoke rising from a stack behind, photographed in colour against a pale sky.
historical_images.caption: The batch house at an Owens-Corning Fiberglas plant in Toledo, Ohio, February 1942, storing the raw materials melted down into the glass fiber that unsaturated polyester resin would soon be paired with.
historical_images.author: Alfred T. Palmer

historical_images.alt: A white fiberglass sailboat moored beside an older varnished wooden sailboat of the identical hull design, in a marina with other boats in the background.
historical_images.caption: A fiberglass and a timber-built Folkboat, same hull design, side by side — the direct comparison unsaturated polyester eventually made possible for an entire category of small craft.
historical_images.author: Packhorse

density.conditions: At 20°C, cured base resin. Mark's Polymer Data Handbook reports a broader specific-gravity range for cast forms (rigid 1.04-1.46, flexible 1.01-1.20).

dielectric_constant.conditions: 1 MHz, cast (unfilled) resin; molded compounds 3.2-4.5, glass-fiber-reinforced ≈5.

electrical_conductivity.conditions: Reciprocal of reported volume resistivity (1×10¹⁴ Ω·cm = 1×10¹² Ω·m).

water_absorption.conditions: Equilibrium, immersion in water at 23°C. Mark's Polymer Data Handbook reports 0.15-0.6% for cast rigid forms (24 h, 1/8 in. sample).

synthesis.industrial_process_notes: Polyester research at DuPont began in 1926 under Wallace Carothers; the unsaturated-polyester approach was patented in Britain in 1928 by General Electric. Two-stage process: (1) polycondensation of a diol with an unsaturated dicarboxylic acid to form the base unsaturated polyester, then (2) free-radical crosslinking with a vinyl monomer (typically styrene) initiated by an organic peroxide, producing a 3-D crosslinked thermoset network.

crystallinity_typical.conditions: Amorphous crosslinked thermoset network once cured; Mark's Polymer Data Handbook classifies UP as a thermoset polymer system (mixture of unsaturated polyester prepolymer with a vinyl monomer).

hdt.conditions: 1.82 MPa, cast rigid (unfilled) grade; glass-fiber-reinforced grades reach 157-287°C.

thermal_conductivity.conditions: Base/cast resin. Glass-fiber-reinforced grades reported far higher (2.6-8.4 W/(m·K)) per Mark's Polymer Data Handbook, reflecting filler content.

tensile_modulus.conditions: Cast base resin. Mark's Polymer Data Handbook reports a broader cast-rigid range (2,100-4,400 MPa) and much higher glass-fiber-reinforced values (5,500-31,000 MPa).

tensile_strength_at_break.conditions: Cast base resin. Mark's Polymer Data Handbook reports 4.1-90 MPa for cast rigid and up to 340 MPa for glass-fiber-reinforced (woven cloth) grades.

elongation_at_break.conditions: Cast base resin. Mark's Polymer Data Handbook reports <2.6% for cast rigid and 40-310% for cast flexible grades.

impact_izod.conditions: Cast, rigid (unfilled); cast, flexible >370 J/m; glass-fiber-reinforced 80-1,600 J/m.

hardness.conditions: Cast, rigid (unfilled); cast, flexible Shore D84-94; glass-fiber-reinforced Barcol 40-80.

flexural_modulus.conditions: Cast base resin. Mark's Polymer Data Handbook reports 3,400-4,200 MPa for cast rigid (296 K) and 7,000-21,000+ MPa for glass-fiber-reinforced grades.

weathering_uv.value: Good weathering resistance (general property of unsaturated polyester thermoset systems).

processing_methods: hand lay-up / spray-up (with glass fiber reinforcement)

processing_temp_range.conditions: Glass-fiber-reinforced compression/injection/transfer molding compounds (SMC/BMC/prepreg); wide range reflects different molding forms and process types. Hand lay-up/cast UP without heated molding is typically cured near room temperature with a peroxide catalyst. Replaces an earlier not-applicable judgement -- heated molding is a real process for glass-fiber-reinforced UP compounds.

shrinkage_rate.conditions: Unfilled resin, linear mold shrinkage. Glass-fiber-reinforced 0.02-1.2%; SMC as low as 0.002%.

environmental.environmental_notes: As a thermoset composite (typically glass-fiber reinforced), end-of-life disposal is difficult; mechanical grinding for use as filler is the main reuse route rather than true recycling.
